title: Git & the Pull-Request Workflow
summary: **Git** tracks changes as commits on branches; teams collaborate by branching, opening **pull requests**, reviewing, and merging. Fluency here is assumed on day one of any job.

subtopics.title: Commits & branches
subtopics.explanation: A commit is a snapshot with a message; a branch is a movable pointer so you can work without disturbing main.

subtopics.title: Pull requests
subtopics.explanation: You push a branch and open a PR: a reviewable diff with discussion, checks, and approval before merging to main.

subtopics.title: Merge vs rebase
subtopics.explanation: Merge preserves history with a merge commit; rebase replays your commits on top of main for a linear history. Don't rebase shared branches.

subtopics.title: Code review
subtopics.explanation: Small, focused PRs with a clear description get reviewed faster and catch bugs before production.

foundations.overview: Git is a distributed version-control system that records your work as commits on branches. Teams collaborate through the pull-request workflow: branch off main, commit, push, open a PR, get it reviewed, pass CI checks, and merge. Knowing this flow — plus resolving conflicts and choosing merge vs rebase — is table-stakes for working on any team.
foundations.formalDefinition: Git is a content-addressable version-control system; a repository is a graph of commits, each a snapshot with a parent. Branches are named pointers into that graph.
foundations.whyItMatters: Every team ships through Git and PRs. Weak Git fluency (giant PRs, messy history, fear of conflicts) slows a whole team and is visible in interviews and on the job.
foundations.mentalModel: A save-game system with timelines: commits are saves, branches are parallel timelines, and a PR is asking to merge your timeline into the main one after review.
foundations.browserPerspective: Not browser-specific, but it's how the code that becomes your frontend gets integrated and shipped.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Feature branches, PR review, resolving merge conflicts, reverting a bad deploy, and reading git blame/log to understand history.
foundations.businessImpact: Good PR hygiene speeds delivery and reduces production incidents; bad Git practice causes lost work and broken main branches.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Small reviewable PRs, meaningful commits, and clean history make the codebase maintainable and onboarding faster.
foundations.performanceImpact: N/A directly, but CI runs on PRs and gates merges, tightening the feedback loop.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Rebase is always better than merge.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Rebase gives linear history but rewrites commits — never rebase a branch others are working on; merge is safer for shared branches.
Large PRs are slower to review and hide bugs; small, focused PRs merge faster and safer.

theory.question: Explain the pull-request workflow and when you'd merge vs rebase.
theory.directAnswer: You branch off main, commit focused changes, push, and open a PR — a reviewable diff where teammates comment and CI runs. After approval and green checks you merge. Merge creates a merge commit and preserves the true history; rebase replays your commits on top of the latest main for a clean linear history. I rebase my own local feature branch to stay current, but I never rebase a branch others share, and I prefer merge (or squash-merge) into main for traceability.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The team integration model on top of Git.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It's how all real work ships; interviewers probe it to gauge collaboration maturity.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: PRs gate merges with review + CI; merge vs rebase is a history-shape tradeoff.

theory.whyImportant: Poor Git practice is a direct team-velocity and reliability risk.

nestedTopics.title: Squash merge
nestedTopics.explanation: Collapses a PR's commits into one tidy commit on main — common for keeping history readable.

followUps.question: How do you resolve a merge conflict?
followUps.answer: Pull the latest main, reproduce the conflict, edit the marked regions to the correct combined result, test, then commit the resolution — don't blindly accept one side.

keyTakeaways: Branch off main, commit, push, open a PR, review, pass CI, merge.
Commits are snapshots; branches are movable pointers.
Merge keeps history; rebase linearizes it — don't rebase shared branches.
Small, focused PRs are reviewed faster and catch more bugs.
git revert/reset and blame/log are your recovery and investigation tools.
